text: ELEGOO UNO R3 controller board (Arduino Uno R3 compatible) (part number No formal ELEGOO MPN found. Confirmed va; on the kit lid: UNO R3 Controller Board). Category: microcontroller Aliases: Arduino Uno R3; ELEGOO UNO R3; UNO R3 clone board Function: This is the brain of the kit: a small board that runs the program you write and controls every wire connected to it. It reads sensors, decides what to do based on your code, and sends signals out to turn on lights, spin motors, move servos, and more. Looks like: Rectangular PCB about 7 cm x 5.5 cm, with a USB-B port and a round DC barrel power jack on one short edge, and a row of black plastic pin-header sockets along each long edge. Most ELEGOO boards are blue soldermask (some are black); a black rectangular IC sits in the middle (either a wide DIP-28 through-hole chip or a small square surface-mount chip, depending on revision); a small silver 3-legged crystal/resonator sits near it; a small square reset button is near the USB port; a few tiny surface-mount LEDs sit near the USB connector (a steady power LED and a blinking TX/RX pair). Printed text: Silkscreen reads "UNO R3", "ARDUINO" or "ELEGOO" plus pin labels above each header: POWER (NC, IOREF, RESET, 3V3, 5V, GND, GND, VIN), ANALOG IN (A0-A5), and DIGITAL (SCL, SDA, AREF, GND, D13 down to D0, with a tilde ~ before PWM-capable pin numbers 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11). Easily confused with: Arduino Mega 2560 (larger board, many more pins); other-brand Uno R3 clones with an identical header layout; ELEGOO Mega board

Pin 1: There is no single numbered pin 1; the board exposes four separate pin-header strips instead of one connector. The power header (NC, IOREF, RESET, 3V3, 5V, GND, GND, VIN) sits on the short edge next to the USB-B connector and the round DC barrel jack. The analog header (A0-A5) runs along one long edge. The digital header (SCL, SDA, AREF, GND, D13 down to D0) runs along the opposite long edge, with the SCL/SDA/AREF end nearest the reset button and the D0/D1 end nearest the USB port. The 6-pin ICSP header is its own 2x3 pin block near the middle of the board, next to the ATmega328P chip. Polarity sensitive: True. Electrical: operating_voltage: 5V logic (on-board 5V regulator output); absolute_max_voltage: 20V on the VIN barrel jack (Arduino Uno Rev3 input voltage limit); exceeding this risks damaging the onboard regulator; typical_current: roughly 45-50 mA idle board draw; varies with attached peripherals (rule-of-thumb figure, not independently confirmed for the ELEGOO clone); max_current: 20 mA max per digital I/O pin, 50 mA max on the 3.3V pin (official Arduino Uno Rev3 spec, assumed to apply to the ELEGOO clone); logic_level: 5V TTL/CMOS; interface: digital, analog (ADC), PWM, UART, I2C, SPI (multi-interface microcontroller board) Key specs: microcontroller: ATmega328P; microcontroller_chip_pin_count: 28 pins in the DIP-28 through-hole package (seen on the ATMEGA16U2-USB kit revision per an Amazon listing), or 32 pins in the surface-mount TQFP/MLF package (seen on the CH340C kit revision confirmed via 3DJake). This is the ATmega328P chip's own package pin count, separate from pins.pin_count (38), which counts the board's exposed header pins (power, analog, digital, and ICSP).; clock_speed: 16 MHz; flash_memory: 32 KB (0.5 KB used by bootloader); sram: 2 KB; eeprom: 1 KB; digital_io_pins: 14; pwm_pins: 6; analog_input_pins: 6; usb_to_serial_chip: CH340C (standalone ELEGOO board, confirmed) or ATMEGA16U2 (some kit bundle revisions, per Amazon listing). Safety hazards: Reversed-polarity power into the barrel jack (center must be positive) can damage the board; Static discharge can damage exposed chip pins; Shorting 5V to GND on the header can overheat the onboard regulator Handling: Hold the board by the edges of the PCB; Do not touch chip legs or header pins with wet hands; Unplug USB power before attaching or removing a shield Common mistakes: Feeding more than the rated ~20V into the barrel jack; Drawing more than 20 mA from a single digital pin (for example wiring an LED with no series resistor); Uploading code while something else is driving D0/D1 (RX/TX), which interferes with the USB programming connection Troubleshooting: symptom: Board not recognized by the computer; likely_cause: Missing USB driver for the CH340 or ATMEGA16U2 chip, or a bad USB cable; check: Check Device Manager (Windows) or System Information (macOS) for a COM/serial port when plugged in; symptom: Power LED not lit; likely_cause: No power reaching the board (bad cable, reversed barrel-jack polarity, blown regulator); check: Measure voltage between the 5V and GND header pins with a multimeter; symptom: Code uploads but nothing happens; likely_cause: Wrong board or COM port selected in the IDE, or a bug in the sketch; check: Re-select "Arduino Uno" and the correct port in the IDE, then re-upload Multimeter test: With the board powered (USB or barrel jack), set the meter to DC volts and measure between the 5V pin and any GND pin; expect close to 5.0V. Measure between 3V3 and GND for close to 3.3V.

16x2 character LCD display module (HD44780-type) (part number 1602A; on the kit lid: LCD1602 Module (with pin header)). Category: display Aliases: 1602 LCD; 1602A LCD; 16x2 LCD Function: A small screen that displays two lines of up to 16 letters or numbers, so your project can show text instead of just blinking lights. Showing sensor readings, menus, a clock, or status messages from your Arduino program. Looks like: A rectangular glass display window (roughly 80mm x 36mm) mounted on a slightly larger PCB, with a single row of 16 pin holes along the bottom edge. The kit's "with pin header" label means a straight breakaway male header ships either pre-soldered or loose alongside it. Screen background is usually solid blue or blue-green with white or black characters when lit; the PCB is typically green or blue. Printed text: Silkscreen near the header often reads "1602A" or similar, with pin numbers 1-16 printed above or below the header holes. Easily confused with: 16x2 LCD with an I2C backpack (only 4 pins: GND, VCC, SDA, SCL, plus a small blue potentiometer on a separate small board); 20x4 LCD modules (larger, 4 lines); monochrome graphic LCDs (128x64, no visible character grid lines)

16x2 character LCD display module (HD44780-type) (part number 1602A; on the kit lid: LCD1602 Module (with pin header)). Safety hazards: Backlight can get warm with prolonged use; Reversing VDD/VSS can damage the controller chip; Forcing current through the backlight the wrong way can damage the LED Handling: Handle by the PCB edges, avoid pressing on the glass display area; Keep RW tied to GND unless your code actually reads the busy flag Common mistakes: Forgetting the contrast potentiometer, which makes the screen look blank or full of black boxes; Wiring RS and E backwards; Leaving RW floating instead of grounded, which can cause erratic behavior Troubleshooting: symptom: Screen is blank but backlight is on; likely_cause: Contrast (V0) not adjusted, or wrong pin numbers in code; check: Turn the contrast potentiometer while the board is powered; you should see rows of black boxes appear; symptom: Backlight does not light at all; likely_cause: No power reaching VDD/VSS or the backlight pins, or reversed backlight polarity; check: Measure voltage between VDD and VSS with a multimeter; expect about 5V; symptom: Garbled or random characters; likely_cause: Wrong wiring on the data pins (D4-D7) or RS/E, or the sketch is set up for the wrong pin mapping; check: Double check each data pin against the sketch's LiquidCrystal() constructor pin list Multimeter test: With the module powered, measure DC voltage between VDD (pin 2) and VSS (pin 1); expect about 5V. Measure between A (pin 15) and K (pin 16) for the backlight supply; expect close to the supply voltage minus the resistor's voltage drop.

UNO prototype shield with SYB-170 mini breadboard (part number generic proto shield with SYB-170 mini b; on the kit lid: Prototype Expansion Module). Category: tool Aliases: proto shield; prototyping shield; expansion board Function: A blank circuit board that plugs on top of the UNO and gives you a small breadboard and solder pads, so you can build a circuit without a tangle of loose wires. Building semi-permanent or compact circuits: stick components onto the small breadboard on top for a solderless build, or solder parts directly onto the prototyping grid underneath for something sturdier. Looks like: A rectangular PCB the same footprint as the Uno (about 7cm x 5.5cm) with two rows of female header sockets on the underside that plug straight down onto the Uno's pins, and a small breadboard (about 4.8cm x 3.4cm) stuck on top with its own grid of tiny insertion holes. PCB color usually matches other boards in the kit (commonly blue or red); the mini breadboard on top is white plastic with a printed red stripe (positive rail) and blue stripe (negative rail) along its edges. The header sockets are silkscreened with the mirrored Uno pin names: SCL, SDA, AREF, GND, 13 down to 8 on one row, 7 down to 0 continuing it, and IOREF, RESET, 3V3, 5V, GND, GND, VIN plus 0 through 5 (analog) along the opposite edge. Printed text: A grid of prototyping pads near the header edges, plus a small reset button and an unlabeled general-purpose push button near one corner, and the pin names above each header row (SCL/SDA/AREF/GND/13-8/7-0 on the digital side, IOREF/RESET/3V3/5V/GND/GND/VIN/A0-A5 on the power/analog side). Easily confused with: A full-size solderless breadboard (much bigger, no header pins to plug into a board); A bare Uno shield with no breadboard on top; A perfboard/stripboard (bare copper pads, no adhesive breadboard on top)

Safety hazards: Misaligning the header pins when pressing the shield onto the Uno can bend a pin; Careless soldering on the prototyping grid can bridge adjacent pads and short a signal to power or ground Handling: Line up the header sockets carefully before pressing down; press evenly, not on one corner; Unplug USB power before attaching or removing the shield Common mistakes: Assuming the mini breadboard's power rails are automatically connected to the Uno's 5V/GND (they are not, until you jumper them yourself); Forgetting the shield adds height, which can make some enclosures not fit Troubleshooting: symptom: Nothing on the shield's breadboard works; likely_cause: The breadboard's power rails were never jumpered to the Uno's 5V/GND pins; check: Run a jumper wire from a 5V pin on the shield header to the breadboard's + rail, and GND to the - rail, then re-check; symptom: Uno stops responding after attaching the shield; likely_cause: A bent or misaligned header pin is shorting two signals together; check: Remove the shield and inspect the header pins for bending before reseating Multimeter test: With the shield seated and the Uno powered, measure continuity between any GND point on the shield's header and the Uno's own GND pin; you should read near 0 ohm, confirming a solid connection.

MB102 breadboard power supply module (part number MB102; on the kit lid: Power Supply Module). Category: power Aliases: MB-102; breadboard power supply; solderless breadboard PSU Function: A little board that turns a 9V battery or wall adapter into clean, steady 5V and 3.3V power for your breadboard circuits. Powering breadboard circuits without needing the Uno or a USB cable connected; useful when you want a project to run on its own. Looks like: A small rectangular PCB, about 5.3cm x 3.3cm, with two rows of pin headers along its long edges spaced to plug straight into a standard breadboard's end power rails, and a round barrel jack plus a USB-A port sticking out one end. Usually a blue PCB with white silkscreen; two small black switches near the middle for jumper voltage selection; a small LED that lights when powered. Printed text: Silkscreen near the header pins usually reads "5V", "3.3V", and "GND" or +/- symbols, plus "MB102" printed on the board. Easily confused with: A generic USB charging module (no barrel jack or breadboard-pin footprint); A single-rail voltage regulator breakout; A relay module (similar size, but has a large relay can and screw terminals instead of breadboard pins)

5V SPDT relay (part number SRD-05VDC-SL-C; on the kit lid: 5V Relay). Safety hazards: The internal coin cell battery is a swallowing hazard, especially around young children; A loose coin cell can short and heat up if it touches metal objects like coins or keys in a pocket or drawer Handling: Match the battery's polarity to the marking in the battery compartment when replacing it; Remove the plastic pull-tab insulator before first use if the battery ships pre-installed; Keep the remote out of direct sunlight and high heat, since coin cells and plastic housings degrade faster when hot Common mistakes: Forgetting to remove the battery insulator tab, so the remote appears dead out of the box; Aiming the remote away from the receiver's sensor window, or standing too far away or at too steep an angle; Assuming the remote works through walls or other solid obstructions; infrared needs a mostly clear line of sight Troubleshooting: symptom: Remote does nothing, no response from the project; likely_cause: Battery insulator tab still in place, or battery dead or missing; check: Open the battery compartment and confirm a battery is seated and any pull-tab has been removed; symptom: Some buttons work but others do not; likely_cause: Worn or dirty membrane contacts under specific buttons; check: Press firmly and squarely on the button; if it still fails, the remote itself likely has a fault; symptom: Receiver only responds at very close range; likely_cause: Weak or low battery, or receiver misaligned; check: Swap in a fresh CR2025 coin cell and re-test at a normal distance and angle Multimeter test: A multimeter cannot read the remote's infrared light output directly. 830 tie-point solderless breadboard (part number commonly labeled MB-102, an industry-gen; on the kit lid: 830 Tie-Points Breadboard). Category: tool Aliases: MB-102 breadboard; full-size breadboard; plug-in breadboard; protoboard Function: A plastic board full of spring-loaded holes that lets you connect electronic parts together temporarily, with no soldering. Building and testing circuits quickly. You push component legs and wire ends into the holes, and hidden metal clips join the right holes together so current can flow, the same as a soldered connection but removable. Looks like: A flat, rectangular plastic board about 165 mm long, 55 mm wide, and 8 to 9 mm thick, roughly the size of a large smartphone. Covered in a precise grid of small square holes. Usually white or off-white ABS plastic. Two long rows of holes at the very top edge and two at the very bottom edge are marked with a red line and + symbol (one rail of each pair) and a blue or black line and - symbol (the other rail). A wide unmarked gap runs down the center of the board, splitting the main grid into upper and lower halves. Printed text: Small printed column numbers along the top of the main hole grid and row letters along one side, silkscreened directly onto the plastic. A peel-off label naming the kit or brand may be stuck to the underside metal backing plate. Easily confused with: smaller half-size or mini breadboards (170 or 400 tie points, roughly half the length); the small prototype breadboard built into the kit's own prototype expansion module; a plain plastic ruler at a glance, before the hole grid is visible up close

Each column of 5 holes is one electrically joined node, used to plug in a component leg or wire. Not connected to the lower half.; pin: circuit area, lower half; name: 63 columns x 5 holes; role: component tie-points; notes: 315 holes, mirrors the upper half. A center gap running the length of the board separates upper and lower halves; nothing crosses that gap internally.; pin: top power rail pair; name: 2 rows x 50 holes; role: power distribution; notes: 100 holes. One row is marked with a red stripe/plus sign (intended for a positive supply), the other with a blue or black stripe/minus sign (intended for ground). All holes along one marked row are joined into a single long node.; pin: bottom power rail pair; name: 2 rows x 50 holes; role: power distribution; notes: 100 holes, mirrors the top pair. The top and bottom rail pairs are separate nodes from each other unless a wire bridges them. Pin 1: There is no pin 1. Orientation is read from the printed + and - symbols and red/blue color stripes next to the two power rail rows at the top and bottom edges. A wide unmarked center gap running the long way across the board splits the main circuit area into an upper and lower half that are not connected to each other. Polarity sensitive: False. 830 tie-point solderless breadboard (part number commonly labeled MB-102, an industry-gen; on the kit lid: 830 Tie-Points Breadboard). Safety hazards: none inherent to the board by itself; a rail can become a shock or fire risk only if a circuit plugged into it exceeds the board's 36V/2A per-contact rating or shorts across a power rail Handling: keep the board dry, the internal spring clips can corrode; do not force oversized leads (thicker than about 0.7 mm, thinner than 21 AWG wire is fine) into the holes, it can permanently spread the internal clips and ruin that hole's grip; peel and stick the metal backing plate to a flat surface if the board needs to stay in place Common mistakes: assuming the upper and lower halves of the main circuit area are electrically joined across the center gap; they are not; assuming all four power rail rows are tied together; the top pair and bottom pair are usually separate unless bridged with a wire; plugging a component's two legs into what looks like one column but is actually split across the center gap, leaving the circuit open Troubleshooting: symptom: circuit does not work even though the wiring looks right; likely_cause: a component leg landed one column off from where a jumper wire is, so they are not actually in the same 5-hole node; check: recount columns carefully, or test continuity between the two holes with a multimeter; symptom: intermittent connection, circuit cuts out when the board is bumped; likely_cause: a spring clip has worn out after repeated use (rated for about 50,000 insertions) or a lead was too thick or thin for a solid grip; check: move the same wire to a fresh, unused column and see if the fault follows the wire or stays with that spot on the board; symptom: part of the circuit has no power; likely_cause: assuming the left and right (or top and bottom) power rails are joined together when they are actually separate rail pairs; check: run a multimeter continuity test along the rail between the point being powered and the point being supplied Multimeter test: Set the multimeter to continuity or resistance mode. Touch one probe to a hole and the other probe to a hole you believe is in the same node (same 5-hole column, or same power rail row). A beep or a reading near 0 ohms confirms they are connected. No beep means they are not connected, or the spring clip has failed.

USB A to B cable (part number not applicable, generic commodity cable ; on the kit lid: USB Cable). Category: wiring Aliases: USB 2.0 printer-style cable; Arduino programming cable; USB A-B cable Function: This is the cable that plugs the Arduino board into a computer so the computer can power it and load programs onto it. It connects a computer's USB port to the Arduino UNO board. Through this one cable, the computer both powers the board and sends it a new program (this is called 'uploading a sketch'). Looks like: A cable roughly 3 to 6 feet long with two different plugs on each end. One end is a flat, wide plastic plug (USB Type-A). The other end is a smaller, squarish plug with two gently rounded top corners (USB Type-B). Cable jacket is usually black, white, or grey. Connector shells are usually silver-grey metal. No polarity markings are needed because the shape prevents wrong-way insertion. Printed text: Cables rarely have printed text; occasionally 'USB 2.0' or 'Hi-Speed' is printed near one of the connectors or on the jacket. Easily confused with: USB printer cables (identical Type-A to Type-B shape, this is the same cable style); USB-A to Micro-USB or USB-A to USB-C cables, which have a much smaller, flatter connector on the device end instead of the squarish Type-B plug

USB A to B cable (part number not applicable, generic commodity cable ; on the kit lid: USB Cable). Pin count: 4. Pinout: pin: 1; name: VBUS; role: power; notes: Carries 5 volt power from the computer or USB power adapter to the Arduino board.; pin: 2; name: D-; role: data (negative); notes: Paired with D+ as a twisted pair inside the cable to carry data while resisting electrical noise.; pin: 3; name: D+; role: data (positive); notes: Paired with D- as a twisted pair inside the cable to carry data while resisting electrical noise.; pin: 4; name: GND; role: ground / return; notes: Common return path for both the power and the data signals. Pin 1: There is no separate step to find pin 1 by eye. The connector shells are shaped so the cable only fits one way: the flat, wide end (USB Type-A) plugs into the computer, and the squarish end with slightly rounded top corners (USB Type-B) plugs into the Arduino board. Because the plastic shell is keyed like this, it is physically impossible to insert either end backwards, unlike a battery where you must check + and -. Polarity sensitive: False. USB A to B cable (part number not applicable, generic commodity cable ; on the kit lid: USB Cable). Safety hazards: Low voltage (5V), not a shock hazard under normal use.; Forcing a connector in upside down can bend or break the internal pins if someone tries to force a mismatched or misaligned plug. Handling: Never force the connector; if it does not slide in easily, check you have the right end and the right orientation.; Unplug by pulling the plastic shell, not the cable jacket, to avoid damaging the wires inside. Common mistakes: Trying to power the board from a phone charge-only cable that lacks the two data wires, which will power the board but prevent uploading a program.; Using a very long or low-quality cable, which can cause upload errors or an unrecognized device. Troubleshooting: symptom: Board powers on (lights up) but the computer does not recognize it as a device; likely_cause: The cable may be a charge-only cable missing the D+ and D- data wires, or the cable/port is faulty; check: Try a different, known-good USB A-B cable and a different USB port on the computer; symptom: Uploads fail partway through or are unreliable; likely_cause: Poor quality or damaged cable, or a bad connection; check: Reseat both ends firmly, try a shorter cable, and check for a 'device disconnected' message in the computer's device list while wiggling the cable gently Multimeter test: With one end unplugged, set a multimeter to continuity mode and touch one probe to the VBUS pin (pin 1) on the Type-A end and the other to the VBUS pin on the Type-B end; a beep or near-zero-ohm reading confirms that wire is intact. Repeat for GND (pin 4). The D+ and D- wires are hard to test this way for actual data function, since continuity alone does not prove they carry data correctly.

check: Verify the longest leg goes to GND, move it there if it was on 5V; symptom: Only some colors light up; likely_cause: A resistor or jumper wire is missing or loose on one or more color legs, or that pin is not being driven in the sketch; check: Use a multimeter to check continuity from the Arduino pin through the resistor to the LED leg, and confirm the sketch writes to that pin; symptom: Colors look dim or washed out; likely_cause: Resistor value is too high, or the PWM duty cycle in the sketch is too low; check: Measure voltage across the LED leg while PWM is active, and compare the resistor's value to the typical 220 ohm reference; symptom: One color is noticeably dimmer than the others at the same PWM level; likely_cause: Different color dies have different forward voltages, red is lower than green or blue, so identical resistors make red appear brighter or dimmer than the others depending on wiring; check: This can be normal behavior, try a different resistor value on the mismatched color leg to balance perceived brightness Multimeter test: Set the multimeter to diode-test mode. Put the black (COM) probe on the longest leg (the common cathode) and touch the red probe to each of the other three legs in turn. Each color die should light dimly and the meter should show a forward-voltage-like reading, red typically the lowest, green and blue typically similar and a bit higher. If a color die does not light during this test, that die is likely damaged or that leg was misidentified.

10K NTC thermistor (part number none printed on the part, generic NTC 10; on the kit lid: Thermistor). Category: sensor Aliases: NTC thermistor; 10K thermistor; temperature sensor resistor Function: A small two-wire part whose electrical resistance changes with temperature, so Arduino can measure temperature by measuring resistance. In this kit it is used for the temperature-sensing lesson, for example a simple thermometer readout or a temperature-triggered project such as a fan that turns on when it gets warm, read through one analog input pin on the Arduino. Looks like: A small round or teardrop-shaped bead, roughly 3 to 5 mm across, with two thin wire leads coming out of the bottom, mounted through-hole like a tiny bead on two wires. Usually a dark epoxy coating (black, dark blue, or gray) with bare tinned copper leads. Printed text: Usually none. Unlike a resistor it has no color bands, and unlike an IC it has no printed part number. Easily confused with: a resistor, but a resistor is a small cylinder with colored bands, while this part is a round bead with no bands; a photoresistor (LDR), but a photoresistor has a flat top with a visible zig-zag light-sensing surface, while this part is a smooth solid blob with no visible sensing pattern; a small ceramic disc capacitor, which has a similar bead-like shape but a flatter disc profile and sometimes printed markings

10K NTC thermistor (part number none printed on the part, generic NTC 10; on the kit lid: Thermistor). Pin count: 2. Pinout: pin: 1; name: Lead A; role: resistive element terminal; notes: either lead, interchangeable, no polarity; pin: 2; name: Lead B; role: resistive element terminal; notes: either lead, interchangeable, no polarity Pin 1: There is no pin 1 or positive lead to find. Both wire leads are electrically identical and can be connected either way around. Polarity sensitive: False. Electrical: operating_voltage: not applicable in the usual sense, it is a passive resistor, not a powered part. It works at whatever voltage is present in the divider circuit, typically Arduino's 5V analog rail; absolute_max_voltage: not specified by any datasheet found, limited in practice by self-heating rather than a voltage rating; typical_current: well under 1 mA in a typical 5V, 10k ohm voltage-divider circuit with Arduino; max_current: not specified, keep current low (a few mA or less) to avoid self-heating, which makes the temperature reading run high; logic_level: not applicable, this is an analog passive component, not a logic device; interface: analog Key specs: resistance_at_25c_ohms: 10000; beta_b25_50_kelvin: 3950; tolerance_resistance: approximately plus or minus 1 percent, per a similar retail 10K/3950 thermistor, ELEGOO's exact tolerance is not confirmed; operating_temperature_range_c: -55 to 125, typical for generic 10K/3950 NTC thermistors, not confirmed for the exact ELEGOO-bundled part Wiring to UNO: example_connections: part_pin: Lead A; uno_pin: 5V; part_pin: Lead B; uno_pin: A0, and to one leg of a fixed 10k ohm resistor; part_pin: fixed 10k ohm resistor, other leg; uno_pin: GND; required_extra_parts: one fixed resistor, commonly 10k ohm, to complete the voltage divider; arduino_library: none required, read with the built-in analogRead() function and convert to temperature using the Beta equation in the sketch's own code

10K NTC thermistor (part number none printed on the part, generic NTC 10; on the kit lid: Thermistor). Safety hazards: No electric shock risk at Arduino's low 5V; very high external heat can crack or melt the epoxy bead Handling: the two wire leads are thin and can fatigue or break if bent back and forth at the same spot; no polarity, so it cannot be plugged in backwards; avoid pushing more than a few mA through it, extra current causes self-heating that makes the reading inaccurate Common mistakes: wiring it alone without the companion fixed resistor, so the analog pin just reads a fixed rail voltage instead of a changing one; using a B-value or resistor value in the code's formula that does not match the one actually wired in, which throws off the computed temperature; mistaking it for a photoresistor since both are small unlabeled two-lead sensors Troubleshooting: symptom: analog reading is stuck near the top (about 1023) or bottom (about 0); likely_cause: missing the companion divider resistor, or a broken or loose connection; check: confirm a fixed resistor completes the voltage divider and both leads are firmly connected; symptom: temperature reading is wildly wrong or does not change at all; likely_cause: wrong B-value or divider-resistor value used in the sketch's formula, or a bad connection; check: measure the resistance across the two leads directly with a multimeter and compare to the expected 10k ohm at room temperature; symptom: reading slowly climbs while the circuit sits untouched; likely_cause: self-heating from too much current flowing through the thermistor; check: measure the divider current, and increase the fixed resistor value or reduce supply voltage if the current is too high Multimeter test: Disconnect the thermistor from the circuit, set the multimeter to resistance (ohms) mode, and measure across its two leads. At room temperature, about 25 C, expect roughly 10,000 ohms. Warm the bead slightly, for example by holding it between two fingers, and the reading should drop. Let it cool and the reading should rise again, confirming normal NTC behavior.

1N4007 rectifier diode (part number 1N4007; on the kit lid: Diode Rectifier). Category: passive Aliases: 1N4007G (Pb-free / lead-free version); General purpose rectifier diode; Flyback diode / freewheeling diode (this kit's usage, not the part's generic name) Function: A diode is a one-way valve for electric current: it lets current flow easily in one direction, from the anode to the cathode, and blocks it in the other direction. In this kit it is mainly used as a flyback diode, also called a freewheeling diode, wired backwards across a relay coil or motor. Coils and motors are inductive loads, meaning that when the current driving them is suddenly switched off, the collapsing magnetic field creates a brief high-voltage spike in the opposite direction. The diode sits reverse-biased (blocking, doing nothing) during normal operation, but that voltage spike forward-biases it for an instant, giving the spike a safe path to dissipate instead of destroying the transistor or Arduino pin that was driving the coil. The same part can also rectify, meaning convert AC to pulsing DC, in a basic power supply, though that is not how this kit's tutorial uses it. Looks like: Small cylindrical body about 5.2mm long and 2.7mm in diameter, roughly the size of a grain of rice, with two thin wire leads extending straight out from each end (each at least 25mm long before any bend). Solid black or dark gray epoxy body with a single light gray or white stripe/band painted near one end. That band marks the cathode lead. Printed text: 1N4007 printed in small white or gray text along the body. Some units also show a date code (year and work week) and a small manufacturer logo. Easily confused with: 1N4001 through 1N4006 (identical black cylindrical body and stripe marking, differ only in the printed number and reverse-voltage rating); 1N4148 / 1N914 small-signal switching diode (similar stripe marking but a much smaller clear glass body, not black plastic, and cannot handle 1A); Zener diodes in the same DO-41 package (look externally identical, only the printed part number and a datasheet lookup tell them apart)

1N4007 rectifier diode (part number 1N4007; on the kit lid: Diode Rectifier). Pin count: 2. Pinout: pin: 1; name: Cathode; role: Current exits here during forward conduction. This is the terminal marked by the painted stripe/band on the body.; notes: In flyback wiring across a coil, this lead connects toward the positive/supply side of the coil so the diode stays reverse-biased in normal operation.; pin: 2; name: Anode; role: Current enters here during forward conduction. This is the unmarked end, with no stripe.; notes: In flyback wiring, this lead connects to the switched node, for example the collector of the transistor or relay driver that pulls the coil low. Pin 1: Look for the single light-colored stripe or band painted around the body near one end. The lead closest to that stripe is the cathode. This is a bare through-hole part, not a module, so there is no printed pin-1 marker other than the stripe. Polarity sensitive: True. Electrical: operating_voltage: Not a powered/logic part. When forward-biased (conducting) it drops about 0.93V typical (1.1V max) at 1A. When reverse-biased it blocks voltage up to its rated maximum (see absolute_max_voltage).; absolute_max_voltage: 1000V VRRM (peak repetitive reverse voltage); 1200V VRSM (non-repetitive surge reverse voltage, half-wave single-phase 60Hz); 700V VR(RMS).; typical_current: Up to 1.0A average rectified forward current (IO), single-phase resistive load, 60Hz, 75 degrees C ambient.; max_current: 30A non-repetitive peak surge current (IFSM) for one 8.3ms half-cycle (60Hz surge rating). Continuous current above 1.0A average is outside the rated spec.; logic_level: not_applicable; interface: none Key specs: package_case: DO-41 outline (onsemi Case 59-10), axial-lead, epoxy molded, about 0.4 gram; VRRM_peak_reverse_voltage: 1000 V; VRSM_surge_reverse_voltage: 1200 V (half-wave, single phase, 60 Hz); VR_RMS_reverse_voltage: 700 V; IO_average_forward_current: 1.0 A (resistive load, 60 Hz, ambient 75 C); IFSM_peak_surge_current: 30 A for one cycle; VF_forward_voltage_drop: 0.93 V typical, 1.1 V max, at 1.0A forward current, 25 C junction temperature; VF_AV_max_full_cycle_average: 0.8 V max; IR_reverse_leakage_current: 10 uA max at 25 C junction temp; 50 uA max at 100 C junction temp; operating_storage_temp_range: -65 C to +150 C; body_dimensions: 4.10 to 5.20 mm long, 2.00 to 2.70 mm diameter (0.161 to 0.205 in by 0.079 to 0.106 in); lead_length_min_each_side: 25.4 mm (1 inch) Wiring to UNO: example_connections: part_pin: Cathode (striped end); uno_pin: Not wired to an Arduino pin directly. Connects to the positive/supply-side terminal of the relay coil or motor (the same node as the coil's Vcc / flyback supply connection).; part_pin: Anode (unstriped end); uno_pin: Not wired to an Arduino pin directly. Connects to the switched node, i.e. the relay driver transistor's collector or the motor driver output, so the diode is reverse-biased during normal operation and only conducts during the coil's turn-off voltage spike.; required_extra_parts: Relay module or DC motor (the inductive load the diode protects); NPN transistor or MOSFET driving the coil, if building a discrete driver instead of using a relay module; External power supply appropriate for the relay/motor coil; arduino_library: none. The diode is a passive protection component; it is not addressed by Arduino code.

1N4007 rectifier diode (part number 1N4007; on the kit lid: Diode Rectifier). Safety hazards: Not a shock or fire hazard by itself at hobby voltages, but if installed backwards (reversed polarity) across an inductive load, it will not block the flyback voltage spike, letting that spike damage the driving transistor or an Arduino pin.; If driven well beyond its 1A / 1000V ratings, for example wired directly across a live AC mains circuit without a current-limiting load, it can overheat and rupture. Handling: Do not bend the leads sharply right at the body. Bend at least a few millimeters away from the body to avoid cracking the glass-passivated junction inside.; Leads conduct soldering heat toward the body. Avoid holding a lead near the body for more than a few seconds while soldering. Common mistakes: Installing the diode with the stripe (cathode) on the wrong side, which reverses its polarity and defeats its job as a flyback diode.; Leaving the flyback diode out entirely across a relay coil or motor, letting inductive voltage spikes reach and potentially damage the driving transistor or Arduino pin.; Confusing it with a similarly shaped small-signal diode, such as a 1N4148, which cannot handle 1A of current. Troubleshooting: symptom: Relay driver transistor (or motor driver IC) fails repeatedly after a period of use; likely_cause: Missing flyback diode, or diode installed backwards, so the coil's turn-off voltage spike is not being clamped; check: Visually confirm the diode is present across the coil with the cathode stripe toward the supply/positive side. Verify polarity with a multimeter diode test.; symptom: Diode measures as an open circuit in both directions; likely_cause: Diode has failed open, usually from an excessive voltage spike or current surge; check: Multimeter diode test in both directions. A good diode reads roughly 0.5 to 0.8V one way and open (OL) the other.; symptom: Diode measures as a short circuit in both directions; likely_cause: Junction failure from overcurrent or reverse-voltage breakdown; check: Multimeter diode test. If shorted, replace the part, and check the upstream circuit for whatever caused the overcurrent or overvoltage before powering back up. Multimeter test: Set the multimeter to diode test mode (the diode symbol). Touch the red lead to the anode (unstriped end) and the black lead to the cathode (striped end): a good diode shows roughly 0.5 to 0.8V forward voltage drop. Reverse the leads: a good diode shows an open circuit (OL). If both directions read near 0V, the diode is shorted; if both read OL, it is open, either way it needs replacing.

light-dependent resistor (LDR) (part number GL5528; on the kit lid: Photoresistor (Photocell)). Category: sensor Aliases: LDR; CdS cell; photocell; photoconductive cell Function: It is a small light sensor whose resistance drops as the light around it gets brighter, so an Arduino can read it to tell how bright or dark a room is. Sensing ambient light level for projects like automatic night lights, light-triggered alarms, or dimming controls. It is wired into a voltage divider (a pair of resistors that splits a voltage) so the changing resistance turns into a changing voltage that the Arduino can measure. Looks like: A small, flat, roughly circular disc about 5 mm across and under 2 mm thick, with two thin bare wire leads exiting from the same edge of the disc, running parallel to each other. The disc face is typically orange-red or reddish-brown with a visible zig-zag (serpentine) light-sensitive track pressed into the surface, sometimes covered by a thin clear or translucent coating. There is usually no printed part number legible on the tiny part itself. Printed text: Generally none readable on the component. The part identity (e.g. GL5528) is normally only found on the kit's parts bag, tray label, or tutorial booklet, not stamped on the part. Easily confused with: NTC thermistor: a small rounded bead or blob on two leads (no flat disc, no visible zig-zag surface); small ceramic disc capacitor: similar flat disc silhouette on two leads, but usually blue, tan, or brown with no zig-zag pattern, and it is not light sensitive

light-dependent resistor (LDR) (part number GL5528; on the kit lid: Photoresistor (Photocell)). Pin count: 2. Pinout: pin: 1; name: Lead 1; role: sensor terminal, no polarity; notes: electrically identical to lead 2, can go to either side of the voltage divider; pin: 2; name: Lead 2; role: sensor terminal, no polarity; notes: electrically identical to lead 1, can go to either side of the voltage divider Pin 1: There is no pin 1 or polarity to find, both leads are electrically identical and interchangeable. Identify the part itself by its small flat disc (about 5 mm across) with a visible zig-zag light-sensitive track on its face, and two bare wire leads coming out of the same edge of the disc. Polarity sensitive: False. Electrical: operating_voltage: No supply voltage of its own; it is a passive resistor used as one leg of a voltage divider, commonly wired into a 5V divider on the Uno.; absolute_max_voltage: 100 V DC (Vmax, the maximum voltage that may be applied continuously while the part is in darkness, per the GL55-series datasheet); typical_current: Not given as a device rating. Current through the part depends on the divider resistor value, the supply voltage, and the light level, since it is a variable resistor, not an active component.; max_current: Not stated directly. Bounded indirectly by the 100 mW maximum power rating (Pmax) at the applied voltage.; logic_level: Not applicable, this is a passive analog resistive sensor, not a logic-level device.; interface: analog Key specs: photo_resistance_at_10_lux: 8 kOhm to 20 kOhm (GL5528, measured at 10 lux per the GL55-series datasheet); dark_resistance: 1.0 MOhm minimum (measured 10 seconds after the light is removed, per datasheet); spectral_peak: 540 nm (green light, close to the peak sensitivity of the human eye); response_time: typical rise time ~45 ms, typical fall time ~55 ms; max_power_rating: 100 mW (Pmax); photoconductive_material: CdS (cadmium sulfide); package_dimensions: about 5.1 mm head diameter, 4.3 mm head width, 1.8 mm thick, leads 3.4 mm apart, lead length ~36 mm, lead diameter ~0.5 mm Wiring to UNO: example_connections: part_pin: Lead 1; uno_pin: 5V; part_pin: Lead 2 (divider midpoint, also joined to one leg of a fixed resistor whose other leg goes to GND); uno_pin: A0; required_extra_parts: one fixed resistor to complete the voltage divider (commonly 10 kOhm in typical Arduino tutorials; the exact value used in ELEGOO's own kit tutorial could not be confirmed in this research pass because elegoo.com blocked automated fetches); arduino_library: none required, read directly with analogRead() on an analog input pin

light-dependent resistor (LDR) (part number GL5528; on the kit lid: Photoresistor (Photocell)). Safety hazards: None significant at hobbyist voltages, this is a low-voltage passive component; Contains cadmium sulfide (CdS), the light-sensitive material inside the disc. Do not crush, burn, or ingest the part, and dispose of it as electronic waste rather than household trash if it breaks Handling: No electrostatic discharge (ESD) sensitivity concerns like there are with chips; The two leads are thin and can fatigue or snap if bent sharply and repeatedly right at the base of the disc Common mistakes: Expecting a simple on/off (digital HIGH/LOW) signal, when it actually needs a voltage divider and an analog reading; Wiring it alone to an analog pin with no second resistor, which gives a reading that barely changes with light; Mistaking it for a thermistor and expecting it to respond to temperature instead of light Troubleshooting: symptom: analogRead() always returns nearly the same value no matter the light level; likely_cause: the fixed divider resistor is missing, or there is an open or shorted connection; check: confirm a second resistor completes the divider between the sensor node and ground or 5V, then check continuity on both leads with a multimeter; symptom: the reading moves opposite to what the code expects (goes down in bright light instead of up, or vice versa); likely_cause: the divider is wired with the photoresistor on the opposite leg from what the sketch assumes; check: trace which lead goes toward 5V and which goes toward GND/A0, and match that to the sketch's logic; symptom: reading is stuck near 0 or near the maximum value regardless of light; likely_cause: a short or open circuit in the sensor itself or its partner resistor; check: disconnect the sensor and measure resistance directly across its two leads in bright light and then fully covered Multimeter test: Set the multimeter to resistance (ohms) mode and measure directly across the two leads with the part disconnected from the circuit (or at least isolated). Under normal indoor room light, expect roughly 8 to 20 kOhm (thousands of ohms) for this part at a moderate 10 lux brightness. Fully cover the disc so no light reaches it, and the reading should climb to over 1 MOhm (millions of ohms).

PN2222A NPN general-purpose transistor (part number PN2222A; on the kit lid: NPN Transistor PN2222). Category: passive Aliases: PN2222; PN2222A; 2N2222; 2N2222A; MMBT2222A (surface-mount version) Function: A tiny electronic switch that lets a weak signal from the Arduino turn a bigger current on or off. In this kit it is used to let a small 5V signal from the UNO control something that needs more current than an Arduino pin can safely supply, such as a relay coil or a small motor. It can also amplify a weak signal. Looks like: Small black plastic part shaped like a half-cylinder, roughly 5mm wide and 5mm tall (TO-92 package), with a flat face on one side and a rounded back, and three thin wire legs coming straight down from the bottom in a single row spaced about 1.27mm apart. Solid black (sometimes dark grey) plastic body. The part number is usually printed in small light-colored text on the flat face. Printed text: PN2222A (sometimes shortened to PN2222 or shown as an equivalent like 2N2222) printed on the flat side of the case. Easily confused with: Other TO-92 transistors such as the 2N3904 or 2N2222, which look visually identical; the printed part number is the only reliable way to tell them apart; Small 3-terminal voltage regulators, which use the same black TO-92-style body

PN2222A NPN general-purpose transistor (part number PN2222A; on the kit lid: NPN Transistor PN2222). Pin count: 3. Pinout: pin: 1; name: E; role: Emitter; notes: Usually wired toward ground (ground side of the load path).; pin: 2; name: B; role: Base; notes: The control input. Drive this from an Arduino pin through a series resistor (about 1k Ohm), never straight from the pin.; pin: 3; name: C; role: Collector; notes: Usually wired to the negative side of the load being switched. Pin 1: Hold the transistor with the flat printed face toward you and the three wire legs pointing down. Reading left to right in that orientation, the legs are Emitter, Base, Collector (E-B-C), per the onsemi/Fairchild datasheet's TO-92 pin diagram. Polarity sensitive: True. Electrical: operating_voltage: Not self-powered; it switches whatever voltage the load circuit uses, up to its maximum ratings below. The base can be driven directly from a 5V Arduino digital pin through a base resistor.; absolute_max_voltage: Collector-Emitter (VCEO): 40V. Collector-Base (VCBO): 75V. Emitter-Base (VEBO): 6.0V.; typical_current: Datasheet describes it as suited for medium-power switching and amplifying up to about 500 mA of collector current in typical use.; max_current: 1.0 A absolute maximum collector current (IC).; logic_level: Base-emitter turn-on voltage is roughly 0.6-0.7V, compatible with a 5V logic HIGH from an Arduino digital pin through a base resistor.; interface: digital Key specs: package: TO-92, 3 leads; dc_current_gain_hFE: Ranges from 35 to 300 depending on collector current and test conditions (e.g. hFE is at least 100 at IC=150mA, VCE=10V); max_power_dissipation: 625 mW at 25C ambient, derated 5.0 mW per additional degree C; gain_bandwidth_product: 300 MHz minimum; collector_emitter_saturation_voltage: 0.3V typical at IC=150mA, IB=15mA (rises to 1.0V at IC=500mA, IB=50mA); storage_and_junction_temperature_range: -55C to +150C Wiring to UNO: example_connections: part_pin: Base (pin 2); uno_pin: A digital output pin (e.g. D9) through a series base resistor of about 1k Ohm; part_pin: Emitter (pin 1); uno_pin: UNO GND; part_pin: Collector (pin 3); uno_pin: Not connected directly to the UNO; wired to the negative/return side of the load being switched (for example, a relay coil or small motor), with the load's other side going to the external supply; required_extra_parts: A base resistor, about 1k Ohm, in series between the Arduino pin and the base; A flyback diode (such as the kit's 1N4007) placed across any inductive load like a relay coil or motor to protect the transistor; arduino_library: none; controlled directly with digitalWrite() or analogWrite() on the pin driving the base resistor

PN2222A NPN general-purpose transistor (part number PN2222A; on the kit lid: NPN Transistor PN2222). Safety hazards: Wiring the collector and emitter reversed, or connecting the base directly to 5V without a resistor, can overheat and permanently damage the transistor; Switching an inductive load such as a motor or relay coil without a flyback diode across it can produce a voltage spike large enough to destroy the transistor Handling: Bend the leads gently and well away from the plastic body; bending right where the lead meets the body can crack the internal seal; The three leads are close together, so check for solder bridges after soldering Common mistakes: Treating it like a simple on/off switch and skipping the base resistor; Mixing up the base and collector legs since all three leads look identical; Confusing an NPN part like this one with a PNP part, which is wired the opposite way Troubleshooting: symptom: The load never turns on; likely_cause: Base resistor value too high, base wired to the wrong pin, or a bad connection; check: With the Arduino pin driven HIGH, measure the voltage at the base leg relative to the emitter; it should read about 0.6 to 0.7V; symptom: The transistor gets hot or smells burnt; likely_cause: Missing base resistor, reversed collector/emitter wiring, or a missing flyback diode on an inductive load; check: Power off immediately, let it cool, and recheck the wiring against the E-B-C pinout before reapplying power; symptom: The load stays on all the time even when the Arduino pin is LOW; likely_cause: Collector and emitter leads swapped, or a solder bridge shorting two legs together; check: Visually inspect solder joints and confirm each leg lands in the correct breadboard row Multimeter test: Set the multimeter to diode-test mode. Touch the red probe to the base and the black probe to the emitter, then to the collector; each should show a diode-like forward drop of about 0.5 to 0.7V. Reverse the probes and both readings should show open circuit (OL). This confirms two working NPN junctions from the base.

Left unused in ELEGOO's basic tutorial wiring either way.; pin: 3; name: SCL; role: I2C clock; notes: Wire to the Arduino Uno's SCL pin (analog pin 5), per ELEGOO's own tutorial.; pin: 4; name: SDA; role: I2C data; notes: Wire to the Arduino Uno's SDA pin (analog pin 4), per ELEGOO's own tutorial. Open-drain and needs an external pull-up resistor; most breakout boards include this pull-up onboard.; pin: 5; name: VCC; role: power in; notes: Wire to the Arduino Uno's 5V pin, per ELEGOO's own tutorial. See electrical.operating_voltage: the safe input range depends on which chip is actually populated, so treat this as 5V-only unless the chip marking confirms DS3231.; pin: 6; name: GND; role: ground; notes: Wire to the Arduino Uno's GND pin. Pin 1: No numbered pin 1. The six pins are printed left to right on the header as 32K, SQW, SCL, SDA, VCC, GND, per ELEGOO's own tutorial wiring diagram. The coin-cell battery holder is the other clear identifying feature, and its size is itself a strong clue: a large, round CR2032 holder (20 mm across) points to a DS3231/ZS-042 board; a smaller CR1220 holder (12.5 mm across) points to ELEGOO's separately-listed "DS1307 Module V03" spare part. Polarity sensitive: True. Electrical: operating_voltage: Depends on the actual populated chip, which this second pass narrowed but did not fully close. If the module is a DS3231 (now the better-supported identification): 2.3V to 5.5V, so it works safely down to 3.3V logic (per lastminuteengineers.com's DS3231 module reference). If the module is a genuine DS1307: 4.5V to 5.5V only, not safe to rely on at 3.3V (per the DS1307 datasheet). Because the chip cannot be told apart from a photo alone, treat any unconfirmed unit as 5V-only until the printed chip marking is read; running an unconfirmed board at 3.3V will not damage a DS3231 but may simply fail to work on a genuine DS1307, which is a safe way to narrow it down further (see troubleshooting).; absolute_max_voltage: -0.5V to +7.0V on any pin relative to ground (DS1307 datasheet, Dallas Semiconductor/Analog Devices). This figure is for the bare DS1307 chip; a DS3231-based board's absolute maximum was not separately confirmed this pass, so do not exceed 5.5V on VCC regardless of which chip is installed.; typical_current: up to 1.5 mA active supply current at 100 kHz SCL clocking (DS1307 datasheet); 300 nA typical battery-backup current at 25 degrees C with the oscillator running and SQW/OUT off (DS1307 datasheet). These figures are for the bare DS1307 chip only; DS3231-specific current figures were not confirmed by a fetched source this pass, so if the module turns out to be a DS3231 these numbers may not apply.; max_current: 1.5 mA active supply current maximum, 200 microamp standby current maximum, 500 nA battery-backup current maximum at 25 degrees C (DS1307 datasheet). Same caveat as typical_current: confirmed for the DS1307 chip only.; logic_level: 5V nominal on the header either way; SDA and SQW/INT are open-drain and need an external pull-up, normally already present on the breakout board. A DS3231-based board can additionally run its logic down to 3.3V (see operating_voltage); a genuine DS1307-based board cannot.; interface: I2C Key specs: timekeeping_fields: seconds, minutes, hours, day of week, date, month, year, with automatic leap-year correction valid through the year 2100 (DS1307 datasheet; the DS3231 provides the same set of fields over the same I2C interface).; backup_ram: 56 bytes of battery-backed nonvolatile RAM built into the DS1307 chip (DS1307 datasheet). Not confirmed for a DS3231-based board, which instead commonly carries a separate AT24C32N EEPROM chip on the same PCB for user data storage (see below); the DS3231 chip itself has no equivalent onboard RAM.; oscillator: external 32.768 kHz quartz crystal, 12.5 pF load capacitance (DS1307 datasheet, applies to the bare DS1307 chip).; i2c_speed: up to 100 kHz, standard-mode I2C (DS1307 datasheet).; backup_battery: Most likely a CR2032 lithium coin cell (the larger, 20 mm size). Second-pass source: an independently revised copy of this exact kit's tutorial on GitHub describes this same lesson's board as a "ZS-042 Module aka. DS3231 RTC Module with AT24C32N EEprom chip and CR2032 battery," and a search-engine snippet of ELEGOO's own current wiki page for the same lesson uses nearly identical wording. A separate, genuinely ELEGOO-branded spare-part listing for a "DS1307 Module V03" specifies the smaller CR1220 cell instead, so a CR1220 holder on a physical unit points to that different part.; onboard_eeprom: Likely an AT24C32N I2C EEPROM chip (32 kilobit / 4 kilobyte) sharing the module's I2C bus, commonly found on DS3231/ZS-042 boards (per an independently revised copy of this kit's tutorial on GitHub, which lists an "AT24C32N datasheet.pdf" file alongside this lesson's materials). Not confirmed for a genuine DS1307-based ELEGOO module. If the marking cannot be read, note the coin-cell size (CR2032 leans DS3231, CR1220 leans DS1307), then power the module from 3.3V logic instead of 5V and run an I2C scanner: a DS3231 will typically still respond at 3.3V, while a genuine DS1307 usually will not respond reliably below its 4.5V minimum. 22 pF ceramic disc capacitor (part number not specified by ELEGOO, generic part wi; on the kit lid: Ceramic Capacitor 22pF). Category: passive Aliases: 22pF capacitor; crystal load capacitor; 22pF disc cap Function: A tiny capacitor that stores a very small electric charge and is almost always used in a matched pair to help a quartz crystal start up and keep steady time. This kit does not wire it into a single named lesson by itself. Its standard job, and the reason it is bundled at all, is as a load capacitor on the two legs of a quartz crystal on a microcontroller. The ATmega328 datasheet lists 12-22 pF as its recommended crystal load capacitor range, which is why kits built around the ATmega328 (the chip on the UNO) include 22pF capacitors. Looks like: A small flat disc or rounded teardrop shape, roughly 5-6 mm across, with two straight wire leads coming out the bottom, spaced about 0.1-0.2 inch (2.5-5 mm) apart. Body color varies by supplier, commonly blue, yellow/tan, or brown. Printed with the number 22 (sometimes followed by a tolerance letter like J or K). Printed text: 22 Easily confused with: 104 ceramic capacitor: same disc shape and through-hole leads, but marked '104' instead of '22' and usually a visibly larger body since it holds much more capacitance; other small-value ceramic discs such as 33 or 47, distinguished only by the printed number
